How can we use this theorem? Well, here are a few remarks:
<STRUCT_0002>
<STRUCT_0003> Suppose that
<MATH_0001> and <MATH_0002> are two morphisms locally of finite
type between locally Noetherian schemes. There is a canonical short
exact sequence
<MATH_0003>
see Morphisms, Lemma <REF_0001>.
The theorem therefore implies that if <MATH_0004> is unramified,
then so is <MATH_0005>. This is
Morphisms, Lemma <REF_0002>.
<STRUCT_0004> Since <MATH_0006> is isomorphic to the conormal sheaf
of the diagonal morphism
(Morphisms, Lemma <REF_0003>)
we see that if <MATH_0007> is a monomorphism of
locally Noetherian schemes and locally of finite type,
then <MATH_0008> is unramified.
In particular, open and closed immersions of locally Noetherian schemes
are unramified. See
Morphisms, Lemmas
<REF_0004> and
<REF_0005>.
<STRUCT_0005> The theorem also implies that the set of points
where a morphism <MATH_0009> (locally of finite type of locally Noetherian
schemes) is not unramified is
the support of the coherent sheaf <MATH_0010>.
This allows one to give a scheme theoretic definition to the
``ramification locus''.
